That work is harder than any road or hydropower project. For generations, we have asked our children to carry our burdens, sending them first to fight real battles and now our economic insecurities. In doing so, we have weakened the very fabric that sustains us.

articles.title: Disappointment and disillusionment for Dalits under the RSP leadership
articles.summary:
What has the Balendra Shah-led government delivered to the traditionally suppressed and marginalised groups, especially Dalits, in its first 100 days in office? Has it raised any hopes of freedom from caste hatred, of social inclusion, of economic prosperity?

I’m afraid not. To the contrary, the Shah administration—by extension, his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP)—seems bent on overlooking Dalit issues and destroying state institutions aimed at liberating Dalits instead. Going down this route, the Balen government may prove to be the most anti-Dalit administration in our democratic history.

Silent settlement of a custodial death

The apparent suicide of Shree Krishna BK in police custody in Sindhuli this April made news headlines. Many people, including Dalit parliamentarians from the RSP, as well as the National Dalit Commission, suspected foul play and demanded an independent investigation into the alleged custodial killing.

Shah himself was in charge of the Home Ministry at the time. He didn’t heed the popular call for justice for the youth suspected of being murdered by the police for marrying a Magar girl. Neither did he meet the victim’s family, nor did he write a single line on his popular social media platforms—nor did he authorise a judicial probe into the case.

Human rights activists have always argued that police investigations into alleged police crimes are never trustworthy. We, therefore, asked for an independent probe, which the government paid no attention to.

In the end, Police Headquarters itself conducted an investigation. Apparently, a report has been presented to the Home Ministry, but it has not been released to the public.

Moreover, the government held secret talks with the victim’s mother and other relatives and made them accept the dead body for cremation. Nobody knows how much was paid and what other benefits were given to BK’s family to settle the alleged murder case outside the court.

No doubt, there have been custodial deaths of Dalit youths in the past. Previous governments, too, have attempted to protect some upper-caste criminals suspected of killing, raping or dominating Dalits. But, at least, the government officials of the day were accessible to the victims’ families and activists. It was then possible to meet people in charge and demand justice.

No longer the case. You might meet gods in the streets of Kathmandu, but not ministers. The Shah administration has no transparency or accountability.

What’s more, Dalit MPs with the RSP have gone extraordinarily quiet. Those who had previously raised a voice for justice for Shree Krishna BK have remained silent since being publicly rebuked by the RSP Chairman Rabi Lamichhane!

Dalit institutions dismantled

The anti-Dalit attitude of the government has become visibly clear with its destruction of two government organisations aimed at promoting Dalit rights and with its clear intentions to destroy the remaining one.

As part of its reform measures, with the stated aim of reducing government spending, the government silently wiped out the Neglected, Oppressed and Dalit Upliftment and Development Committee. Its lengthy and confusing name notwithstanding, it was established primarily to promote the overall development of Dalit communities and to tackle the problem of untouchability.

Likewise, the government closed down the Badi Development Board, which focused on the advancement of the Badi—a Dalit community excluded even by other Dalit communities and which has been further defamed and humiliated owing to the history of their sex work.

No doubt, both of these agencies were not functioning well. Firstly, the officials were yes-men of party leaders and were incompetent; secondly, they were poorly funded. A responsible government that understands the persistent plight of Dalits would attempt to make these organisations efficient and capable—instead of rushing to destroy them for good.

Worse still, the government aims to dismantle the National Dalit Commission (NDC). It has not been destroyed already, only because it is a constitutional body like the Human Rights Commission and the Election Commission. The Balen administration wants to wipe it out for good—if not, make it a branch of the Human Rights Commission.

In all these cases, the justification of minimising state expenditure doesn’t hold. Because, as indicated earlier as well, these agencies have survived on meagre budgets. That’s part of the reason for their lack of effectiveness.

Fake apologies, fake promises

I wrote in this column quite a while ago, arguing that the Balen administration would never offer a state apology to Dalits, and that the eloquent speech of the party chair, Rabi Lamichhane, in parliament would be portrayed as a state apology.

Unfortunately, my prediction turned out to be true. Prime Minister Shah never apologised to Dalits. No formal apology has been passed by his Cabinet, and no notice to that effect has been printed in the official gazette. Meaning that the written and official decision of the first Cabinet meeting to formally apologise to Dalits on behalf of the state was a hoax; it was never meant to be enforced. It proved to be a shameless and cheap political stunt!

That historic Cabinet meeting also decided to put in place certain measures to tackle the persistent problem of caste discrimination. But, to date, nothing has happened. There’s no sign of the prime minister and his ministers, the RSP chair and his central committee, the Dalit MPs considering any tangible projects or plans to curb the issue of caste humiliation and violence.

There’s nothing for Dalits in the government budget. There’s nothing for Dalits in the government policies and programmes.

So, the government seems to have zero interest in resolving the issues associated with a highly rigid and oppressive caste structure. This is not what we’d expected, certainly not from a prime minister who belongs to an oppressed oil-pressing community of southern Nepal and northern India. In the name of pure meritocracy, representation of Dalits and other marginalised groups has also been completely ignored by this administration. Dalits have not been appointed to any influential positions.

I’m sure other marginalised groups too feel similarly left out. The Madheshis have been forgotten, and so have the ethnic and religious minorities, as well as the people of Karnali. The government’s utter disregard for issues of social justice, inclusion and equality is likely to cost a great deal.

articles.title: The record Nepal noticed not
articles.summary:
There is a half-second when a hamstring tears at full sprint, in which the body keeps believing it is still running. Aayush Kunwar was through the bend of the 200 metres at the 2024 National Games—into the straight where the race stops being about speed and becomes about holding your shape while your legs come apart—when the muscle in the back of his right thigh gave way. He pulled up and limped off the track; the race gone, the season with it.

I should explain why that matters now. This July, on a track in Los Angeles, Kunwar ran the 200 metres in 21.87 seconds. The Nepali national record, 21.92 seconds, had stood since 1995–the year he was born. It had outlasted three decades of sprinters who came and went without touching it. Nor did he merely reach it; he ran through it, just the way he has done everything in this sport: Alone, on his own money, with no federation standing behind him. I know this because for years, I lived in the room next to his.

We have been roommates twice, two decades apart. Once as schoolboys in Kathmandu and again in San Francisco, both of us in our twenties, still working out what our lives were going to be. Living beside him taught me what the sport actually asks of a person. I watched him come home from a full day as a financial analyst and go straight to the floor to do the physiotherapy he had taught himself. I filmed him on the university tracks around the city, hoping for sponsors to notice. But the camera caught the smallest part of it. Most of his hours had no audience, and nothing about them looked like much: A man on a borrowed track, running the same repetitions until the light gave out.

What I never worked out, in all those years close to it, was ‘why’. Not why anyone runs, but why he ran like this, at this cost, for a sport that gave back so little and so slowly. He could not tell me, and I don't think he knew himself. What stayed with me was that he ran anyway.

A sport is supposed to give an athlete five things: Coaching, physiotherapy, competition, travel and the money that makes the other four possible. Aayush built each of them himself, from parts. He coached his own recovery over the phone. He turned his body into a long experiment in nutrition, worked out between spreadsheets at his day job. He gathered his competition from other Nepali runners scattered across other countries' tracks. When there was no sponsor, he filmed the work and asked strangers to help fund a plane ticket for it. He is not only a sprinter. He is a one-man federation, a fundraiser, an organiser, a recruiter and an athlete who has spent his best years trying to move an entire country's sport a few inches forward.

So when Nepal could not get its National Games off the ground this year, he did not treat it as someone else's failure to mourn. He organised a race himself. He flew home with running shoes packed around his clothes and gave them to athletes who had none. The sport had not done much for him; he had decided, somewhere along the line, to do something for the sport instead.

There is a plain lesson in his 21.87-second record, and we should not let the celebration bury it. A record does not survive for 30 years because it is superhuman. It survives that long because year after year, nobody is given what they need to chase it. Aayush's whole career is the proof of it, and his run this July is the rebuttal he wrote himself. Imagine what a runner like him does with an actual system behind him. Then imagine how many runners like him we have already lost for the want of one.

He is not done though. There are Asian Games ahead, and World Championships, and he means to be there. But the records were never really the point. For a decade, he has been quiet proof of a single idea that one person, with enough discipline and without permission from anyone, can pick up a country's sport and carry it somewhere new. The record he set this summer will fall one day, and there is a fair chance the man who breaks it will again be the same man who just set it. Until then, he will keep doing what he has always done alone, after the workday, on whatever ground will have him, faster than the country that forgot to build him a track.

articles.title: For Kathmandu’s youths, running is about more than fitness
articles.summary:
Over the years, many youths from Kathmandu are joining running clubs as a part of their regular fitness routines. With Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and Strava popularising the trend, individuals gather mostly to enhance fitness and community, occasionally aligned with charity purposes.

As this active outdoor culture is fostering a community of health conscious individuals, questions remain regarding those it can cater to with its monetary membership requirements.

Kabita Kharel, the founder of Revive Fitness and the owner of Revive Supplements discusses the rise of running clubs in Kathmandu, popular routes, mental health benefits and the membership process.

Why are young people turning to running specifically, over gyms or other sports?

It is happening for several reasons rather than just a growing interest in fitness.

Many young adults work or study long hours and spend much of their time online. Running clubs offer a chance to meet people with similar interests, make friends, and build a routine. For many, the social aspect is as important as the exercise. Unlike other sports, running requires relatively little equipment—a good pair of shoes and comfortable clothing. This makes it accessible to students and young professionals.

Awareness of mental health, cardiovascular fitness, and healthy lifestyles has increased especially after COVID 19. People are more aware about health and fitness all around the world including Nepal. Running is seen as an effective way to reduce stress, improve mood, and stay fit without needing a gym membership.

Instagram, Strava, and TikTok have made running more visible. Sharing race medals, sunrise runs, personal bests, and group photos has encouraged others to join. Kathmandu now hosts more road races, charity runs, and trail-running events than it did a decade ago. These events give runners goals to train for and create excitement around the sport.

Most clubs meet early in the morning or on weekends, making it easy for office workers, entrepreneurs, and students to participate before starting their day. Many members say they initially joined to improve fitness but stayed because running helped them manage stress, anxiety, and work pressure. Group runs also reduce the isolation that some young people experience.

Kathmandu has a large population of young professionals and university students, growing fitness awareness, and an active outdoor culture. Running clubs combine exercise, networking, and recreation in a city where people often seek activities that don’t require expensive memberships.

How much of this is about fitness versus social life?

The answer is both—but for many young people, the community is what keeps them coming back. Group runs create a welcoming environment where everyone—from beginners to experienced runners—can participate. Social media amplifies this sense of belonging by showcasing group photos, achievements, and shared experiences.

Over time, the community becomes the reason they stay. The friendships, encouragement, and routine make it easier to keep showing up—even on days when motivation is low.

What was the running culture here like five years ago compared to now?

Five years ago, Kathmandu’s running scene was much smaller and more niche than it is today.

Earlier, Running was mainly for marathon enthusiasts - military athletes and police training . Most people ran alone for individualism.

Now it’s for everyone including youngsters, professionals, fitness enthusiasts . Today people run in large numbers. A lot of fitness platforms approach office houses, schools and other places to inspire people to stay active, organise trail runs, charity runs, 5km races and host events to attract wider audiences .

Do you think this is a lasting shift in how young Nepalis approach fitness, or a passing trend?

I think it’s more likely a lasting shift than a passing trend. This culture for me looks sustainable because fitness has become part of people’s identity.

For many young Nepalese, fitness is no longer just about losing weight. It’s becoming part of how they spend their free time, make friends, and express themselves. Running clubs, gyms, cycling groups, and hiking communities all reflect this broader lifestyle change.

Health awareness is much higher than it was a decade ago. Young people are more informed about the benefits of exercise for physical and mental health. That awareness is unlikely to disappear.

However, not everyone who joins a running club today will still be running in five years. Some people are drawn by social media trends, Fear of missing out (FOMO), posting race photos and achievements

As with many lifestyle trends, some participants will lose interest once the novelty fades.

Some people say running clubs are more of an 'urban, well-off youth' thing. Would you agree with that, or is that not a fair picture?

I think there’s some truth to that observation.

The recent boom in organised running clubs in Nepal is indeed concentrated among urban, relatively well-off young adults, especially in Kathmandu. However, that doesn’t mean running itself belongs only to that group.

Organised running clubs tend to attract people who live in cities like Kathmandu, Lalitpur, or Pokhara, have predictable work or study schedules, can afford quality running shoes and sportswear, use apps like Strava or Instagram and enjoy the social aspect of group runs and have access to parks, running routes, and organised events.

In that sense, the stereotype has some basis. Running itself is much broader than running clubs. Many of these aren’t part of the social-media-driven running culture at all.

There is also a practical factor. While running is relatively inexpensive compared with many sports, participating in the club culture often involves additional costs such as race entry fees and sometimes coffee or breakfast after group runs.

In other words, the organised running-club movement may currently skew urban and middle class, while running as a sport and form of exercise is much more diverse. Those are two related but different phenomena.

Where do these runs normally happen and how can people participate?

Most organised runs in Kathmandu happen early in the morning (around 5:30–7:00 AM) on weekdays or weekends, when traffic and pollution are lower.

Some of the most popular locations include:

Tundikhel – One of the city’s classic running spots with a relatively flat route, popular for interval training and group meetups.

Bagmati Corridor – Increasingly popular because of its longer uninterrupted stretches, making it suitable for easy runs and tempo workouts.

Swayambhunath and nearby hills – A favorite for trail runners and those looking for hill training.

Patan/UN Park and Jhamsikhel area – Frequently used by running clubs based in Lalitpur.

Shivapuri National Park trails – A weekend destination for longer trail runs and endurance training.

The participation process is usually very easy.

Find a local running club through Instagram, Facebook, or Strava. For example, Kathmandu Running Club has an active Strava community that welcomes new members.

Check their weekly schedule. Many clubs post the meeting point, distance, pace groups, and start time a few days before each run.

Show up a little early with comfortable running shoes and water. Most beginner-friendly clubs don’t require membership for a first run.

Introduce yourself to the organizers. Running clubs are generally welcoming to newcomers and often divide runners into different pace groups so beginners don’t feel left behind.

Many clubs also organise more than just runs, they’ll have coffee meetups, workshops, charity runs, and race training programs, which is one reason they’ve become so popular

articles.title: ‘Nepali cinema needs new stories, not recycled formulas’
articles.summary:
Jiwan Jung Basnyat is an actor from Sunsari. He holds a Bachelor's degree in Film Studies (Acting) from Oscar International College and has been acting in theatres since he was 12 years old.

Basnyat changed schools multiple times by Class 6, following his elder brother, a teacher. It was during this itinerant childhood that he was first introduced to theatre, almost by accident.

In the absence of an established theatre culture in his hometown, his journey began without knowing what ‘theatre’ was, which now has spanned over 200 short films, with 50 of them released and a notable work in recent Nepali film ‘Ramita Ko Pirati’.

With The Post’s Jony Nepal, he spoke about his transition from stage to screen and what it takes for actors to find recognition in today’s Nepali film industry.

What inspired you to move into films from theatre?

Once, while watching the movie ‘Chhadke 1’, I saw Bipin Karki play a character called ‘Bindu’, a gangster from Chitwan. Watching it, I realised how seamless the acting was. I believed Karki was actually from Chitwan. It was only later I found out he was a theater actor. That's when it hit me, theater people can do films too. That connected my interest in film with my continuity in theater.

With this, back when I was in grade 8, I messaged the director of ‘Bhutan’, also the principal of Oscar College.

What do you think Nepali audiences and producers should understand about the effort actors put into acting?

Audiences see and feel what's real, so there's not much for them to understand differently. But producers should focus on proper, wise casting, using a real casting process with auditions and screen tests to see if someone genuinely suits a role, instead of casting based on social media followers and personal networking.

It's frustrating watching someone get a lead role after just a random lip-sync trend clip on TikTok, while others with years of proper training and stage experience don't get a chance.

How important is self-promotion for actors?

Extremely important. This is the age of algorithms and reels. The real issue is that trained actors are being forced into promoting themselves through reels just to be seen at all.

Projects I did two or three years ago were just sitting unused on my drive; once I posted them as reels, offers from films actually started coming in.

Personally, when things were financially tough with no work, no money to pay off debt, not even enough to eat, that's when I posted my first clip. It came from real pain, not from ‘selling sympathy’ as few people called it. That said, there is a negative side to this too, many people post reels purely to chase followers, and some without any acting background end up getting mainstream recognition just for that.

What role do costumes and makeup play in developing the emotional layers for a character?

Makeup plays a big role, but only when used properly. Earlier, I used to focus a lot on the outer look with costume and makeup. But now I understand that it is secondary. The first thing is the character's psychology, their mental state, and what situation they're going through. The same thing can be perceived completely differently by different characters; that emotional layer and inner acting is what I now prioritise, more than outer appearance.

Having said that, to help myself believe in my character’s existence within me, I use music, costume, or even my co-actor's reactions become valuable.

What is your opinion on acting education and training in Nepal?

Film colleges brought technical improvement in cinematography and sound. But lately it has degraded. Short-term acting classes run for a month or two without any proper syllabus, and nobody really knows who's teaching or how qualified they are.

Even Bachelor's programs, which should teach specialisation over four years, struggle to do this properly. They fail to develop real industry connections. In my batch, there were 25-30 acting students, and only one or two are getting to work.

Colleges take fees, teach loosely, and do not help students get connected to the industry afterward.

Why do Nepali films struggle to get recognition?

The main reason is a lack of diversity; everyone copies whatever formula last worked. If ‘Loot’ works, everyone else will make ‘Loot’. Such is the case with ‘Purna Bahadur Ko Sarangi’ and many other Nepali films and trends. There's also a shortage of skilled writers and directors in the mainstream.

Real change needs producers and directors who understand cinema and are willing to trust emerging actors and filmmakers.

It is not that we do not have creative artists with expertise and unconventional vision. As the gap between the producers and us persists, so do quality products in Nepali film industry.

I personally made a portfolio of short films and pitched scripts to directors and producers, but most producers only care about finance, not filmmaking knowledge. They kept saying ‘only Purna Bahadur type films will run’, discouraging new stories. With Nepali films increasingly honing the technicalities, be it cinematography, colour grading or art direction, the lack of narrative uniqueness limits their own creative boundaries and audience.

Where do you see the Nepali film industry in the next 10 years?

There are a lot of possibilities. Talented new writers and directors are emerging, if even one of them breaks through the mainstream recognition, it opens doors for other talents too. If new, creative ideas keep coming, I believe Nepali audiences will embrace new tastes as well.

articles.title: Nepal showcases fashion talent at South Asian summit in Sri Lanka
articles.summary:
The Fashion Designers Center (Council), Nepal, facilitated by South Asian Women Development Forum (SAWDF), represented Nepal at the CCWE Fashion Week and South Asian Summit 2026, hosted by the Ceylon Chamber of Women Entrepreneurs in Sri Lanka on July 18.

Designers Bini Bajracharya of ABiR and Mukta Shrestha of Muku represented Nepal, both showcasing their collections as part of the summit’s celebration of South Asian fashion, craftsmanship, and women-led entrepreneurship.

The CCWE Fashion Week and South Asian Summit brought together designers, entrepreneurs, and cultural leaders from across the region to celebrate creativity and cross-border collaboration among South Asian nations. Nepal’s presence at the event, facilitated through SAWDF and the Fashion Designers Center (Council), underscores the country’s growing presence on the regional fashion stage and highlights the contributions of Nepali women entrepreneurs in the creative industries.

“This is a proud moment for Nepali fashion and for women entrepreneurs across the region,” said a spokesperson for the Fashion Designers Center (Council), Nepal. “Showcasing our collections alongside designers from across South Asia is an opportunity to bring Nepali craftsmanship and design to a wider audience.”

The designers presented their collection at the event’s Grande Finale on the 18th. They reported a warm and overwhelming reception on having presented their local designs at one per presenter.

articles.title: Movie review: Nothing is accidental in ‘Ship of Theseus’
articles.summary:
Jean Renoir once said that a filmmaker makes only one film in their life; they then break it into pieces and make it again. The same is true in Anand Gandhi’s case. Across projects like ‘Tumbbad’ and ‘MAYA’’, Gandhi has repeatedly explored questions of identity, morality and the human condition. Yet his cinematic peak arrived with his first writer-director feature, Ship of Theseus. The film turns 13 today.

Released in 2013, the film explores life, art, identity, meaning, justice and death through three seemingly separate stories. In his interviews, Gandhi regularly speaks about how the answers to the most profound philosophical inquiries can be found in the solace of biology.

‘Ship of Theseus’ is the very manifestation of this notion—it approaches the centuries-old Greek paradox, as well as the classic debates in the Bharatvarshiya domain, in perhaps the most somatic manner possible. And this is the very reason that renders it relevant to its 13th anniversary.

Unlike most films produced in the region that are quick to satisfy their audience with ready-made and often easy-to-digest answers, ‘Ship of Theseus’ throws a heap of questions that stifle its viewers. It compels people to leave theatres with a curious mind, questioning their own beliefs. This, the film does through its characters’ and their choices, dilemmas, action and even inaction.

Gandhi’s characters are as convincing as they are bold. The three main ones—a blind photographer, an ailing monk and a philistine stockbroker—stand as the three pillars that carry the film’s most profound queries.

A common understanding in screenwriting is that characters are not real people, meaning that characters need not be bound by the limitations people face in reality. However, people in Ship of Theseus are as real as possible—they are vulnerable, flawed, stern, fixated, loving, empathetic and, most importantly, contradictory.

The first story begins with Aaliya played by Aida El-Kashef. A photographer who began her career after losing her eyesight to a corneal infection, Aaliya is an artist who commands control over her work. For her, photography is anything but a visual experience with auditory cues and palpability of the result as her main aids.

Aaliya’s unyielding eyesight does not limit her, a feeling that seems likely to grow after her cornea transplant. However, having regained her eyesight, she clicks pictures only to loathe them later.

Aaliya’s is a tale that demands pondering over an artist’s grip over their choices. Does intuition play any part whatsoever in art-making? Must every stroke of brush, every shutter-clicked or every word penned be deliberate? Albeit her debut feature performance, Kashef carries the essence of Aaliya until the very last frame of the film. Her performance rightly aligns with the documentary-like approach the film strives to achieve.

An abrupt, thundering cut transitions into the second story featuring Maitreya. The Jain monk with liver cirrhosis, played by Neeraj Kabi, is also an activist fighting against the unnecessary chemical testing carried out on animals. Maitreya is constantly accompanied by Charvaka, a young lawyer trying to “learn to win an argument from both sides.”

Here, Gandhi draws from the eastern pool of knowledge: In Buddhism, Maitreya is a bodhisattva who is going to descend upon earth to reestablish Dharma, while Charvaka was an Indian philosopher who advocated hedonism and materialism, rejecting the authority of the Vedas.

In the film, these characters personify their namesakes, for Maitreya holds a dualistic perception of the soul and body, and the eventual liberation from the karmic cycle of life and death, while Charvaka carries a sansaaric, more practical, approach to living, enjoying the material luxuries of life.

The final narrative features Navin, the stockbroker, who has recently gone through a kidney transplant. Being the philistine that he is, Navin takes no interest in reading books and has never listened to the vocal runs of Mukhtiyar Ali despite hailing from Rajasthan.

Unlike Aaliya and Maitreya’s obstacles that stem from a deeply personal conviction, Navin’s crisis emerges from someone else’s suffering. His willingness to go beyond borders, risking his own life—not for himself or his kin, but in pursuit of justice—exhibits his moral maturity above others’.

However, among the three protagonists, Shah falls shortest in portraying his character. While the matter concerning Navin is one of the most significant in the film, Shah’s stiff portrayal of the character seems evidently rehearsed and forced, constantly reminding the viewer of the film’s fictitious nature.

Nothing is accidental in ‘Ship of Theseus’—everything comes with a subtext. Arcs taken by Aaliya, Maitreya and Navin are filled with symbolisms waiting to be discovered. Like the frog-and-centipede story that Aaliya narrates: That same centipede crawls into the tale of Maitreya—perhaps, one way of connecting the two narratives.

When Navin’s car and his sidekick get stuck at the gates of poor Shankar’s neighbourhood, for one must be of a certain size to fit through such settlements; when Pankaj Kumar, the Director of Photography, uses a shaft of light to emulate a heavenly illumination falling upon Maitreya; or when the sturdy, red buildings stand tall emulating Maiteya’s firm beliefs—meaning is packed to the brim of this film. And these visual and narrative motifs are what keep the film fresh till today, for every revisit rewards the viewer with a new revelation, an “aha!” moment.

Apart from being a contemplative piece that demands more than just viewer attention, ‘Ship of Theseus’ succeeds in low-budget and guerrilla filmmaking.

Whether in terms of cinematography, soundscape, production design or even the cast, the film strips all the glittery bits of filmmaking down to the basics. Kumar captures the film’s visual mood, pace and texture without any fancy gear.

Cinematography that relies on the basics of light and shadows to paint strong, contrasting images, Kumar aligns the visual aesthetics with the film’s minimal approach. Similarly, Benedict Taylor’s violin breathes life into the film with a soundtrack that embodies the idea of continuum that the film is all about.

But since the film tests only the cognitive rigour of the characters, it lacks the emotional depth that moves its viewers. Placing intellectual payoff above an emotional one makes ‘Ship of Theseus’ an admirable film, but rarely a lovable one.

It being a low-budget production is another area where it comes short. Cutting on the cost, the film relies on a lot of non-actors, some of whom are quite glaringly bad at avoiding eye contact with the camera.

While the use of non-actors does add a sense of innocence, authenticity and rawness to the act, their blunders also constantly throw off viewers. So does the occasional amateur sync sound that’s too hard to ignore. But to get tangled up in its blemishes would be to miss the forest for the trees. In an age where perfection is achieved based on a poorly written prompt, this film reminds us of the humanness of imperfections.

‘Ship of Theseus’ is the result of an effort to draw from centuries-old knowledge systems and translate it into cinema. 13 years after its release, the film's appeal remains not because it settles for easy answers, but for its unwavering knack for asking questions. As long as the questions that have kept us awake at night for centuries endure, ‘Ship of Theseus’ will live on.

Ship of Theseus

Language: English, Hindi

Available on: YouTube

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.
